sachet.g: A small scented cloth bag filled with fragrant material such as herbs or potpourri.

sack.e: From Middle English sak, sek, sach, zech (“bag, sackcloth”), from Old English sacc (“sack, bag”) and sæċċ (“sackcloth, sacking”); both from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from late Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), borrowed from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic, possibly Phoenician or Hebrew.
sack.g: A bag; especially a large bag of strong, coarse material for storage and handling of various commodities, such as potatoes, coal, coffee; or

sack.e: From earlier (wyne) seck from Middle French (vin (“wine”)) sec (“dry”), from Latin siccus (“dry”).
sack.g: A variety of light-colored dry wine from Spain or the Canary Islands; also, any strong white wine from southern Europe; sherry.

sackbut.e: From French sacqueboute, from Middle French sacquer (“to pull”) + bouter (“to push”).
sackbut.g: A brass instrument from the Renaissance and Baroque Eras, and an ancestor of the modern trombone. It was derived from the medieval slide tru

sackcloth.e: From Middle English sakcloth, sekcloth, sekclath, sekklath. By surface analysis, sack + cloth.
sackcloth.g: A coarse hessian style of cloth used to make sacks.

sacred.e: From Middle English sacred, isacred, past participle of sacren, sakeren (“to make holy, hallow”), equivalent to sacre + -ed.
sacred.g: Characterized by solemn religious ceremony or religious use, especially, in a positive sense; consecrated, made holy.

sacrifice.e: From Middle English sacrifice (“act of offering a life or object to a deity; the life or object so offered”), from Anglo-Norman sacrefiz, and Old French sacrifice, sacrifise (modern French sacrifice), from Latin sacrificium (“something offered to a deity, sacrifice”).
sacrifice.g: Originally, the killing (and often burning) of a human being or an animal as an offering to a deity; later, also the offering of an object t

sacrifice.e: From Middle English sacrificen (“to offer a sacrifice to a deity”), from sacrifice (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming infinitives of verbs).
sacrifice.g: To offer (a human being or an animal, or an object) to a deity.

sacrificial.e: Borrowed from Latin sacrificiālis (“sacrificial”), from sacrificium (“sacrifice”), from sacrificus (“sacrificial”), from sacrificō (“sacrifice”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”) + faciō (“do, make”). By surface analysis, sacrifice + -ial.

sacrilege.e: From Middle English sacrilege, from Old French sacrilege, from Latin sacrilegium, from sacrilegus (“sacrilegious”). Sense of “profanation” from late 14th century.
sacrilege.g: Desecration, profanation, misuse or violation of something regarded as sacred.

sad.e: From Middle English sad, from Old English sæd (“satisfied, full, sated, unable to handle more, weary”), from Proto-West Germanic *sad, from Proto-Germanic *sadaz (“sated, satisfied”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂- (“to satiate, satisfy”).

sadden.e: From Middle English saddenen, equivalent to sad + -en.

saddle.e: From Middle English sadel, from Old English sadol, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz (“saddle”). Further etymology uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *sod-dʰlo-.
saddle.g: A seat for a rider, typically made of leather and raised in the front and rear, placed on the back of a horse or other animal, and secured b

saddle.e: From Middle English sadelen (“to put a saddle on (an animal), to saddle”), from Old English sadolian, sadelian, sadilian (“to saddle”), from Proto-Germanic *sadulōną (“to saddle”), from *sadulaz (“a saddle”, noun) (see further at etymology 1) + *-ōną (suffix forming denominative verbs from nouns).
saddle.g: To put a saddle (noun sense 1) on (an animal).

saddlebag.g: A covered pouch, usually one of a pair, laid across the back of a horse, donkey, or mule behind its saddle, or hanging over the rear wheel o

saddlecloth.g: A blanket placed under a saddle, a saddle blanket.

sadly.e: From Middle English sadly; equivalent to sad + -ly.

sadness.e: From Middle English sadnesse, equivalent to sad + -ness.
sadness.g: The state or emotion of being sad.

safe.e: From Middle English sauf, safe, saf, saaf, from Old French sauf, saulf, salf (“safe”), from Latin salvus (“whole, safe”), from Proto-Italic *salawos, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, every”).
safe.g: Not in danger; out of harm's reach.

safeguard.e: From Middle English savegard, from Middle French sauvegarde, from Old French salve garde, sauve garde, reconstructed as safe + guard.
safeguard.g: Something that serves as a guard or protection; a defense.

safekeeping.g: the act of keeping something safe; protection from harm, damage, loss, or theft

safely.e: From Middle English savely; equivalent to safe + -ly.
safely.g: In a safe manner; without risk; using caution above all else.

safety.e: From Middle English savete, from Old French sauveté, from earlier salvetet, from Medieval Latin salvitās, salvitātem, from Latin salvus.
safety.g: The condition or feeling of being safe; security; certainty.

saffron.e: From Middle English saffron, borrowed from Old French safran, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin safranum, borrowed from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān), from Aramaic צפר.
saffron.g: A plant of species Crocus sativus, a crocus.

said.e: From Middle English seide (preterite) and seid, iseid (past participle), from Old English sǣde, sæġde (preterite) and ġesæġd (past participle), equivalent to say + -ed.

sail.e: From Middle English saile, sayle, seil, seyl, from Old English seġl, from Proto-West Germanic *segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą.
sail.g: A piece of fabric attached to a boat and arranged such that it causes the wind to drive the boat along. The sail may be attached to the boat

sail.e: From Middle English sailen, saylen, seilen, seilien, from Old English seġlan, siġlan (“to sail”), from Proto-West Germanic *siglijan, from *siglijaną.
sail.g: To be impelled or driven forward by the action of wind upon sails, as a ship on water; to be impelled on a body of water by steam or other p

sailing.e: From Middle English saylinge, seilinge, variants of sailende, seilende; equivalent to sail + -ing.

sailor.e: Alteration of earlier sailer, from Middle English sailer, sayler, saylere, equivalent to sail + -or. Eclipsed non-native Middle English marinel, marynell (“sailor”) borrowed from Old French marinel (“sailor”).
sailor.g: A person who sails; one whose occupation is sailing or navigating ships or other waterborne craft.

saint.e: From Middle English saint, seint, sainct, seinct, sanct, senct, partly from Old English sanct (“saint”) and confluence with Old French saint, seinte (Modern French saint); both from Latin sānctus (“holy, consecrated”, in Late Latin as a noun, “a saint”), past participle of sancīre (“to render sacred, make holy”), akin to sacer (“holy, sacred”).
saint.g: A deceased person whom a church or another religious group has officially recognised as especially holy or godly; one eminent for piety and

saint.e: From Middle English saynten, seinten, sonten, partly from Anglo-Norman saintir and partly from the noun Middle English seint, seynt (see above).
saint.g: Synonym of canonize: to honor, formally name, or revere as a saint.

sake.e: From Middle English sake (“sake, cause”), from Old English sacu (“cause, lawsuit, legal action, complaint, issue, dispute”), from Proto-West Germanic *saku, from Proto-Germanic *sakō (“affair, thing, charge, accusation, matter”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to investigate”).

sale.e: From Middle English sale, from Old English sala (“act of selling, sale”), from Old Norse sala (“sale”), from Proto-Germanic *salō (“delivery”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“to grab”).
sale.g: An exchange of goods or services for currency or credit.

sale.e: From Middle English sale, sal, from Old English sæl (“room, hall, castle”), from Proto-Germanic *salą (“house, hall”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“home, dwelling, village”). Related also to salon, saloon.

saliva.e: A learned borrowing from Latin salīva (“spittle”), replacing or merging with Middle English salive, salve (“saliva”), from the same Latin source. Further origin uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *salw-, *sal- (“dirt, dirty”), cognate with Old English salu (“dark, dusky”).
saliva.g: A clear, slightly alkaline liquid secreted into the mouth by the salivary glands and mucous glands, consisting of water, mucin, protein, and

salt.e: From Middle English salt, from Old English sealt, from Proto-West Germanic *salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”).
salt.g: A common substance, chemically consisting mainly of sodium chloride (NaCl), used extensively as a food ingredient, seasoning, condiment, and

saltness.e: From Middle English saltenesse, saltnesse, from Old English sealtnes (“saltness”), equivalent to salt + -ness.
saltness.g: The state or quality of being salt; saltiness.

salty.e: PIE word sḗh₂l Inherited from Middle English salti. Equivalent to salt + -y.

salutation.e: From Middle English salutacioun, from Old French salutacion, from Latin salutatio (“a greeting, a wishing health to”), from saluto (“wish one’s health, greet”), from salus (“well-being”).
salutation.g: A greeting, salute, or address; a hello.

salutations.e: The interjection is an application of the noun.

salute.e: Borrowed from Latin salūtō (“to greet; to wish health to”), from salūs (“greeting, good health”), related to salvus (“safe”).
salute.g: An utterance or gesture expressing greeting or honor towards someone, (now especially) a formal, non-verbal gesture made with the arms or ha

salvation.e: From Middle English savacioun, from Old French savaciun, salvaciun, from Latin salvātiō.
salvation.g: The process of being saved, the state of having been saved (from hell).

salve.e: From Middle English salve, from Old English sealf, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu, from Proto-Germanic *salbō, from Proto-Indo-European *solp-éh₂, from *selp- (“salve, ointment”).
salve.g: An ointment, cream, or balm with soothing, healing, or calming effects.
To save (the appearances or the phenomena); to explain (a celestial phenomenon); to account for (the apparent motions of the celestial bodie

same.e: From Middle English same, from Old Norse samr (“same”) and/or Old English same, sama (“same”) in the phrase swā same (swā) (“in like manner, in the same way (as)”), both from Proto-Germanic *samaz (“same”), from Proto-Indo-European *somHós (“same”).
same.g: Not different or other; not another or others; not different as regards self; selfsame; identical.

same.e: From Middle English same, samme, samen, (also ysame, isame), from Old English samen (“together”), from Proto-Germanic *samanai (“together”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one, together”).

sample.e: From Middle English saumple, sample, from Old French essample (“example”), from Latin exemplum.
sample.g: A part or snippet of something taken or presented for inspection, or shown as evidence of the quality of the whole; a specimen.

sanctification.e: From Old French sanctificacion, from ecclesiastical Latin sanctificātionem, from sanctificāre (“to sanctify”).
sanctification.g: The (usually gradual or uncompleted) process by which a Christian believer is made holy through the action of the Holy Spirit.

sanctify.e: From Anglo-Norman seintefier, from Old French saintefier, from Late Latin sānctificō, from Latin sānctus (“holy”) + faciō (“do, make”). Form altered to conform with Latin.
sanctify.g: To make holy; to consecrate; to set aside for sacred or ceremonial use.

sanctuary.e: From Middle English seyntuarie, from Old French saintuaire, from Late Latin sanctuarium (“a sacred place, a shrine, a private cabinet, in Medieval Latin also temple, church, churchyard, cemetery, right of asylum”), from Latin sanctus (“holy, sacred”); see saint.
sanctuary.g: A place of safety, refuge, or protection.

sand.e: From Middle English sond, sand, from Old English sand, from Proto-West Germanic *samd, from Proto-Germanic *samdaz.
sand.g: Rock that is ground more finely than gravel, but is not as fine as silt (more formally, see grain sizes chart), forming beaches and deserts

sand.e: From Middle English sanden, from the noun (see above).
sand.g: To abrade the surface of (something) with sand or sandpaper in order to smooth or clean it.

sandal.e: From Middle English sandal (“sandal”), from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”), of unknown origin. Often mistakenly parsed as related to sand.
sandal.g: A type of open shoe made up of straps or bands holding a sole to the foot

sandal.e: From Middle English sandal (“sandalwood”), from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Medieval Greek σάνδανον (sándanon), σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), from Middle Persian (cndl /⁠čandal⁠/, “sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana, “sandalwood”).

sandbar.g: A ridge of sand caused by the action of waves along a shore.

sandy.e: From Middle English sandi, sondy, sandiȝ, from Old English sandiġ (“sandy”), equivalent to sand + -y.

sanity.e: From Middle English sanite, sanyte, sanytee, from Middle French sanité, from Latin sānitās, from sānus (“healthy”) + -itās (“-ity”). By surface analysis, sane + -ity.

sap.e: From Middle English sap, from Old English sæp (“juice, sap”), from Proto-West Germanic *sap (“sap, juice”) (compare Dutch sap, German Saft, Icelandic safi).
sap.g: The juice of plants of any kind, especially the ascending and descending juices or circulating fluid essential to nutrition.

sap.e: From French saper (compare Spanish zapar and Italian zappare) from sape (“sort of scythe”), from Late Latin sappa (“sort of mattock”). The sense evolution of from “subvert by digging” to “weaken” was influenced by the sense above “drain wood of sap” as trench warfare receded from public conscience.
sap.g: To make unstable or infirm; to unsettle; to weaken.

sapling.e: From Middle English saplyng, seplyng, sapling, equivalent to sap + -ling.
sapling.g: A young tree, larger than a seedling.

sapphire.e: From Middle English saphir, from Old French saphir, from Latin sapphir, sappir, sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros, “precious stone, gem”), from a Semitic language such as Hebrew סַפִּיר (sappī́r, “lapis lazuli”), originally from Assyrian Akkadian šipirtu (“lapis lazuli”).
sapphire.g: A clear deep blue variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.

sardine.e: Borrowed from French sardine (cognate with Spanish sardina, Italian sardina), Latin sardīna; from Ancient Greek σαρδίνη (sardínē).
sardine.g: Any one of several species of small herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil or in tins for food, especially the European sardine (

sardine.e: Pliny states that its name was ultimately derived from Sardis, in Lydia, where the sard was first discovered; but probably ultimately derived from Persian sered ("yellowish-red").

sardonyx.e: From Middle English sardonix, sardonyx (c. 1382), from Latin sardonyx, from Ancient Greek σᾰρδόνῠξ (sărdónŭx).
sardonyx.g: A gemstone having bands of red sard; a variety of onyx or chalcedony.

sari.e: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi साड़ी (sāṛī) / Urdu سَاڑِی (sāṛī)), in turn derived from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀸𑀟𑀻 (sāḍī), from Sanskrit शाटी (śāṭī), from शाट (śāṭa, “strip of cloth”).
sari.g: The traditional dress of women in the Indian Subcontinent; an outer garment consisting of a single length of cotton or silk, most often with

sash.g: A piece of cloth designed to be worn around the waist.

sash.e: From sashes, from metathesis of French châssis (“frame (of a window or door)”), taken as a plural and -s trimmed off by the late 17th century.
sash.g: The opening part of a window, usually containing the glass panes; either hinged to the jamb, or sliding up and down as in a sash window.

satisfaction.e: From Middle English satisfaccioun, from Old French satisfaccion and Latin satisfactiō, satisfactiōnis.
satisfaction.g: A fulfilment of a need or desire.

satisfied.e: From Middle English satisfyed, i-satisfyed, i-satisfied, past participle of Middle English satisfien, equivalent to satisfy + -ed.

satisfy.e: From Middle English satisfyen, satisfien, from Old French satisfiier, satisfier (also Old French satisfaire), from Latin satisfacere, from satis (“enough, sufficient”) + faciō (“to make; to do”).

satrap.e: From Middle English satrape, from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāvan (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.
satrap.g: A governor of a Persian province.

satyr.e: From French satyre, from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos).
satyr.g: A sylvan deity or demigod, male companion of Pan or Dionysus, represented as part man and part goat, and characterized by riotous merriment

sauce.e: From Middle English sauce, from Old French sause, from Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), past participle of saliō (“to salt”), from sal. For the meaning development compare Ancient Greek ἥδυσμα (hḗdusma) ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (whence also English sweet).
sauce.g: A liquid (often thickened) condiment or accompaniment to food.

savage.e: From Middle English savage, from Old French sauvage, salvage (“wild, untamed”), from Late Latin salvāticus, alteration of Latin silvāticus (“wild”, literally “of the woods”), from silva (“forest; grove”).

save.e: From Middle English saven, sauven, a borrowing from Old French sauver, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”).

savour.e: From Middle English savour, from Anglo-Norman saveur, savor, savour, and Old French saveur, savor, savour (modern French saveur), from Latin sapor, from sapiō (“to taste of (something); to have a flavour”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁p-, *sep- (“to taste; to try out”)) + -or (suffix forming third-declension masculine abstract nouns).

From Middle English savouren, savour, from Anglo-Norman savorer, savourer, Middle French savorer, savourer, and Old French savorer, savourer (modern French savourer), from Late Latin sapōrāre, the present active infinitive of sapōrō (“to give flavour, make tasty; to give pleasure”).
savour.g: To detect (a flavour or taste, or food or drink); to taste; specifically, to enjoy or linger on (a flavour or taste, or food and drink); to

saw.e: The noun from Middle English sawe, sawgh, from Old English saga, sagu (“saw”), from Proto-West Germanic *sagu, from Proto-Germanic *sagô, *sagō (“saw”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). The verb from Middle English sawen, from the noun above.
saw.g: A tool used for cutting hard substances, in particular wood or metal.

saw.e: From Middle English sawe, from Old English sagu, saga (“story, tale, saying, statement, report, narrative, tradition”), from Proto-West Germanic *sagā, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, *sagǭ (“saying, story”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷe-, *skʷē-, from *sekʷ- (“to say”).

say.e: From Middle English saien, sain, san, secgan, segen, seien, sein, seiȝen, sugen, sægen, ziggen, from Old English seċġan, secgean, secggan, secggean, seggan, sæċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to say”).
From Middle French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“military cloak”).
say.g: A type of fine cloth similar to serge.

sink.e: From Middle English synken, from Old English sincan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷ- (“to fall, sink”). In the causative sense, it replaced Old English senċan (“make sink”) from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną.
sink.g: To move or be moved into something.

sit.e: From Middle English sitten, from Old English sittan, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).
sit.g: To be in a position in which the upper body is upright and supported by the buttocks.
